mainEntity.name: How many 60 lb bags of concrete are in a cubic yard?

acceptedAnswer.text: It takes exactly 60 bags of 60 lb concrete to make 1 cubic yard (27 cu ft divided by 0.45 cu ft per bag). Contractors typically buy 66 bags per yard to allow for 10% subgrade waste.

mainEntity.name: How many 80 lb and 40 lb bags of concrete make a cubic yard?

acceptedAnswer.text: One cubic yard equals 45 bags of 80 lb concrete (0.60 cu ft each) or 90 bags of 40 lb concrete (0.30 cu ft each) before waste.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy 60 lb or 80 lb concrete bags?

acceptedAnswer.text: 80 lb bags cost 5% to 10% less per cubic foot and require 25% fewer rips, making them standard for crews. For solo DIYers lifting into a wheelbarrow or drum mixer, 60 lb bags reduce fatigue.

mainEntity.name: When is it cheaper to order a ready-mix concrete truck instead of bags?

acceptedAnswer.text: The crossover point is typically 1.5 to 2.0 cubic yards (about 68 to 90 eighty-pound bags). Above 2 yards, ready-mix delivery is usually faster, stronger, and cost-competitive.

mainEntity.name: How many bags of concrete come on a full pallet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard US home-center pallets hold 42 bags of 80 lb concrete (3,360 lbs), 56 bags of 60 lb concrete (3,360 lbs), or 80 bags of 40 lb concrete (3,200 lbs).

mainEntity.name: Is the 30% federal residential solar tax credit still available in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The homeowner-direct 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit under IRC Section 25D expired for residential solar and battery installations placed in service after December 31, 2025. mainEntity.name: What is a realistic solar panel payback period in the US in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a cash-purchased residential system in 2026, realistic payback ranges from 7 to 10 years in high-rate states (California, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York) and 11 to 16 years in moderate-rate Midwest and Southern states ($0.14–$0.17/kWh).

mainEntity.name: How much does net metering affect my solar ROI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under full 1:1 retail net metering, exported electricity offsets grid power dollar-for-dollar. Under reduced export or net billing tariffs (such as California NEM 3.0 without storage), payback can lengthen by 3 to 6 years.

mainEntity.name: Should I replace my roof before installing solar panels?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your asphalt shingle roof has fewer than 10 to 12 years of remaining life. Removing and reinstalling a solar array mid-life for a roof replacement typically costs $3,000 to $6,500.

mainEntity.name: Why do low-interest solar loans often have a worse ROI than cash?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many low-APR 25-year solar loans embed 18% to 30% dealer origination fees directly into the financed principal. Always request the cash quote and compare it against zero-fee financing.

mainEntity.name: What is the Ohio state income tax rate in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under Ohio HB 96, tax year 2026 uses a two-tier flat structure: 0% on Ohio taxable income up to $26,050, and a flat 2.75% on all taxable income above $26,050.

mainEntity.name: What are the 2026 municipal income tax rates in major Ohio cities?

acceptedAnswer.text: Major Ohio city income tax rates are 2.5% in Columbus, Cleveland, Akron, Toledo, and Dayton; 1.8% in Cincinnati; and 2.75% in Youngstown. Unincorporated townships levy 0%.

mainEntity.name: Why is Ohio city tax still deducted on my 401(k) contribution?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under Ohio Revised Code Chapter 718, employee 401(k) deferrals reduce Federal and Ohio state income tax but remain taxable wages for Ohio municipal income tax.

mainEntity.name: What is the Ohio School District Income Tax (SDIT)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Roughly one-third of Ohio school districts levy a voter-approved local income tax (0.5% to 2.0%) based on where you live rather than where you work.

mainEntity.name: How much will I take home on $25 an hour in Ohio?

acceptedAnswer.text: At $25/hr for 40 hours per week ($52,000/yr), a Single worker in a 2.5% Ohio city takes home roughly $1,615 bi-weekly (~$41,990/yr), or ~$1,665 bi-weekly in a 0% township.

mainEntity.name: Does Ohio require overtime pay after 8 hours in a single day?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Under Ohio Revised Code §4111.03 and federal FLSA law, non-exempt workers earn 1.5x overtime only after 40 hours actually worked in a workweek.

mainEntity.name: Can working overtime actually make my paycheck smaller?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. US federal income tax brackets are marginal and Ohio uses a flat 2.75% rate above $26,050 in 2026, so working overtime always increases your net take-home pay.

mainEntity.name: Are Ohio municipal city taxes withheld on overtime pay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Overtime and double-time wages are fully subject to Ohio municipal income taxes such as 2.5% in Columbus, Cleveland, Akron, Toledo, and Dayton or 1.8% in Cincinnati.

mainEntity.name: Does PTO or holiday pay count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold in Ohio?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Only hours actually worked count toward the statutory 40-hour overtime threshold unless an employer handbook or union contract provides otherwise.

mainEntity.name: Is double-time pay required on Sundays or holidays in Ohio?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Neither Ohio law nor the FLSA mandates double-time (2.0x) pay on weekends or holidays; it is strictly an employer policy or union benefit.
